title: Stage 1: Rules
summary: Model orders as records and judge them with a list of pluggable IOrderRule objects.

steps.title: The order desk
body: Over five stages you will build an **order desk**: a console program that reads orders, decides what to do with each one, and reports on all of them. Every stage adds one idea from the course, at the point where the program actually needs it.
Each input line is one order: `id,customer,product,quantity`.
At the end of this stage your program prints:
#2 bob Gadget x0 rejected: quantity must be at least 1
#3 carol Gizmo x2 rejected: Gizmo is discontinued

The interesting part is **how** an order is judged. The shop's policy changes all the time: today gizmos are discontinued, tomorrow a customer is blocked. If every check is an `if` inside the main loop, every policy change means editing that loop. Instead, each check becomes its own small class behind one interface:
string? Check(Order order);   // null = fine, otherwise the reason
The loop holds a `List<IOrderRule>` and asks each one. It never knows which rules exist. Adding a rule is adding a class and one line to the list.

steps.prompt: The loop runs `foreach (var rule in rules) rule.Check(order);` where `rules` is a `List<IOrderRule>` holding a `MinQuantityRule` and a `DiscontinuedRule`. Which `Check` method runs on each pass?
options: The one belonging to the object's real class: `MinQuantityRule.Check`, then `DiscontinuedRule.Check`
`IOrderRule.Check`, which has no body, so nothing happens
Always the first implementation the compiler saw
It does not compile: a list of an interface type cannot hold class objects
steps.explain: Calling through an interface is *polymorphic*: the variable's type says what you can call, the object's actual class decides which code runs. That is exactly what lets the loop stay ignorant of the individual rules.

code: var rules = new List<IOrderRule> { new TooSmall(), new TooBig() };
public string? Check(int quantity) => quantity < 1 ? "too small" : null;
public string? Check(int quantity) => quantity > 10 ? "too big" : null;
steps.explain: Each rule returns `null` when it has nothing to say. `OfType<string>()` keeps only the non-null reasons, so an empty list means every rule was happy.

steps.prompt: Complete a rule that is configured through its constructor.
steps.explain: A class implements an interface with `:`. Passing the product in the constructor means the same class can block any product: `new DiscontinuedRule(Product.Gizmo)`. Returning `null` says *no objection*.

steps.title: Two rules behind one interface
prompt: The starter reads and parses the orders for you: `ParseOrder` returns an `Order`, or `null` for a line it cannot read (those are already reported). Your job is the judging.
1. Declare `interface IOrderRule` with one method, `string? Check(Order order)`, which returns `null` when the order is fine and a reason otherwise.
2. Write `class MinQuantityRule : IOrderRule`, which objects with `quantity must be at least 1` when the quantity is below 1.
3. Write `class DiscontinuedRule : IOrderRule` that takes a `Product` in its constructor and objects with `PRODUCT is discontinued` (for example `Gizmo is discontinued`).
4. At the top, build `var rules = new List<IOrderRule> { new MinQuantityRule(), new DiscontinuedRule(Product.Gizmo) };`
5. In the loop, ask **every** rule. If none objects, print `DESCRIPTION accepted`. Otherwise print `DESCRIPTION rejected: ` followed by all the reasons, in rule order, joined with `; `. Count each.
`Describe(order)` gives the description, such as `#1 alice Widget x3`.
#2 bob Gadget x0 rejected: quantity must be at least 1
#3 carol Gizmo x2 rejected: Gizmo is discontinued

steps.title: Policy changes without touching the loop
prompt: The shop has two new policies. Add them **without changing the loop**: only new classes and new entries in the list.
- `class MaxQuantityRule : IOrderRule`, constructed with the maximum, objects with `quantity over MAX`. Use `new MaxQuantityRule(10)`.
- `class BlockedCustomerRule : IOrderRule`, constructed with a customer name, objects with `customer NAME is blocked`. Use `new BlockedCustomerRule("mallory")`.
The rules run in this order: minimum quantity, maximum quantity, discontinued, blocked customer. All objections are reported, in that order.
#5 mallory Gizmo x0 rejected: quantity must be at least 1; Gizmo is discontinued; customer mallory is blocked
#7 frank Widget x12 rejected: quantity over 10
#8 mallory Widget x2 rejected: customer mallory is blocked
Lines that cannot be read (wrong number of fields, an unknown product, a non-number) still print `line N: cannot read 'TEXT'`, where N counts every line including blank ones.
